power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Incretin-based obesity medications (IOMs), particularly glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 RAs, have transformed obesity treatment by producing substantial weight loss and improvements in cardiometabolic health.

However, achieving and sustaining clinically meaningful weight loss in routine clinical practice remains challenging, underscoring the need to identify approaches that enhance the effectiveness of IOM-based therapies.

Real-world 12-month persistence and adherence to GLP-1-based therapies have historically been suboptimal, with earlier studies reporting persistence rates of 24.5%-32.3%, mean proportion of days covered (PDC) of 51.0%-54.3%, and only 27.2%-29.6% of patients achieving PDC ≥80% [1, 2].

Medication data.
Medication data were extracted from the structured medication records in the electronic health record.
We identified records for semaglutide, tirzepatide, and liraglutide, and extracted the ingredient, dose start and end dates, route, and daily dose.
For each participant, we derived the earliest and latest dose dates, the ingredients used, and the number of distinct ingredients.

Dose escalation was assessed monthly: for each ingredient, the highest daily dose recorded in a calendar month was compared with that of the previous month with a recorded dose, and a month was classified as an escalation month if the dose was higher.
We summarized the number and percentage of escalation months, the maximum dose reached, and the time from the first dose to the maximum dose.

Medication coverage was assessed using the proportion of days covered (PDC), calculated as the number of unique days covered by a GLP-1 dose record divided by the number of days in the 12-month period after the start of the primary Rx pathway.
Overlapping records and ingredient switches were counted once per day, and PDC≥80% was considered high coverage.
Side effects.
Participants self-reported IOM-related side effects through the app as part of daily symptom and biomarker logging.
Reported symptoms included fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and abdominal pain.
Each entry was date-stamped, and we extracted the daily symptom values and the number of entries per symptom.
Side effects were summarized descriptively.
Because logging was voluntary and participant-initiated, the data reflect reported symptoms rather than clinician-adjudicated adverse events.

The primary outcome was 12-month weight change from program enrollment, evaluated using both adjusted body weight change derived from longitudinal mixed-effects models and observed percentage weight loss.
Clinically meaningful weight-loss response was assessed as the proportion of participants achieving ≥5%, ≥10%, ≥15%, and ≥20% weight loss at 12 months.

The primary analysis focused on GLP-1-naïve participants who received a single GLP-1-based active pharmaceutical ingredient (semaglutide or tirzepatide) throughout the 12-month intervention period to minimize the potential influence of prior medication exposure and ingredient switching on weight-loss outcomes.

Ancillary analyses evaluated weight-loss outcomes in the overall prescription cohort and across additional subgroups, including the broader GLP-1-naïve population, participants with prior GLP-1 exposure, and those who switched medication ingredients during follow-up.
Among participants with prior GLP-1 exposure, weight-loss outcomes were further examined separately for single active pharmaceutical ingredient semaglutide and tirzepatide users.

Cumulative weight Nutrients 2025, 17, x FOR PEER REVIEW10 of 36 loss from the pre-GLP-1 reference weight through program enrollment and 12-month follow-up was also evaluated to characterize weight-loss trajectories before and after enrollment.

Secondary outcomes included real-world medication utilization and management (medication adherence, medication ingredient, dose titration, ingredient switching, and documented medication trajectory), a descriptive assessment of reported medication side effects, and exploratory analyses of weight-loss outcomes according to medication adherence assessed by PDCs and ingredient switching.
An exploratory outcome was change in HbA1c from program enrollment to 6 and 12 months among participants in the primary single-ingredient, GLP-1-naïve cohort with available HbA1c values.

Continuous medication-related variables were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, whereas categorical medication utilization variables were compared using the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate.
All statistical analyses were performed using R (version 4.6.1; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

In this real-world cohort of adults receiving incretin-based obesity medication within a continuous remote care program, adding individualized carbohydrate-reduced nutritional therapy to IOM (VINT+IOM) was consistently associated with greater adjusted 12-month weight loss than IOM alone.
This held for GLP-1-naïve participants and those with prior GLP-1 exposure, and for both semaglutide and tirzepatide.
Medication coverage and program retention were high in both pathways despite frequent dose changes and ingredient switching.
These findings should be interpreted against established evidence that real-world obesity pharmacotherapy is considerably more dynamic than the standardized exposure achieved in randomized trials.
Adherence, dose escalation, switching, and discontinuation vary substantially in practice, and this variability is frequently not captured in claims-based analyses.

Earlier real-world studies reported mean PDCs of approximately 51%-54%, with only 27%-30% of participants achieving PDC ≥80% [1, 2], and 12-month GLP-1 persistence estimates ranging from 24.5% in a large claims-based cohort to 58.6% for semaglutide and 64.8% for tirzepatide in more contemporary cohorts [1, 2].

text.text: In contrast, approximately 80% of participants in our cohort achieved PDC ≥80%, and 12-month program retention was 77% with VINT+IOM and 72% with IOM only.
Program retention and medication persistence are distinct measures and cannot be directly compared, but these results appear favorable.

They are also consistent with an earlier analysis by Marshall et al. of commercially insured members who may have also received Virta-supported obesity care through the KeepWell program offered by Prime Therapeutics, in which 90.1% remained on GLP-1 therapy at 6 months with a mean weight reduction of 22.2 lb [20].

text.text: The additional weight loss with VINT+IOM (5.1-11.5 lb across cohorts, approximately 19%-52% greater than IOM only) is consistent with emerging, but still limited, evidence that nutritional strategies, particularly carbohydrate reduction, may add value alongside incretin therapy.
HbA1c also declined in all groups, more with tirzepatide than with semaglutide and numerically more with VINT+IOM than with IOM only.

However, differences between pathways were small and not statistically significant, which is unsurprising given that baseline values were normal (about 5.4-5.5%), leaving very little room for further reduction.
In addition, limited follow-up laboratory data reduced the power to detect between-group differences.

text.text: Together, these studies raise the possibility that carbohydrate-reduced strategies may influence not only the magnitude of weight loss but also its composition, as well as other cardiometabolic outcomes, although most of the published studies on body composition were small or uncontrolled.
Body composition was not assessed in our study, so we cannot determine whether the additional weight loss with VINT+IOM reflects fat or lean mass.

Future studies that include body composition measures would help clarify whether carbohydrate-reduced nutritional therapy affects the quality, and not only the amount, of weight lost with incretin therapy.

Randomized and real-world data generally show greater percentage weight loss with GLP-1 receptor agonists in women.

A 2026 meta-analysis of sex-stratified trials found weight loss was greater among women (10.9%) than men (6.8%), and a real-world tirzepatide cohort reported greater weight loss in women than men at 15 months (15.1% vs 10.7%) [26, 27].

Men lost more absolute weight, which largely reflects their higher baseline weight, while observed 12-month percentage weight loss and most responder rates were similar by sex, and the sex difference did not vary by medication.
A larger male advantage appeared only within VINT+IOM and was not consistent across models.

text.text: These observations indicate that substantial weight loss occurred in routine care among participants who did not reach maximum medication doses.
They do not establish that the therapeutic effect is independent of medication dose or duration of exposure, and we did not evaluate dose-response relationships.
In this setting, medication intensity was adjusted over time according to individual response and tolerability, alongside ongoing carbohydrate-reduced nutritional support from VINT.

Among GLP-1-naïve participants, weight loss with VINT+IOM continued between 6 and 12 months without a clear plateau, suggesting that 12-month outcomes may not represent the maximal treatment response, particularly because initiation and titration occurred during program follow-up.
However, these comparisons with clinical trials and other real-world studies should be interpreted cautiously.
They are descriptive and involve differences in study populations, medication doses, treatment duration, follow-up, and analytic approach.
Substantial additional weight loss was also observed among participants who entered VINT + IOM with prior GLP-1 exposure.

Among prior users remaining on a single ingredient, mean additional weight loss during 12 months of VINT + IOM was 8.8% with semaglutide and 13.8% with tirzepatide, despite pharmacotherapy and associated weight loss having begun before program entry.

text.text: Although differences in populations, medication exposure, adherence definitions, and study designs preclude direct cross-study comparisons, the substantial weight loss observed with VINT+IOM despite prior GLP-1 exposure or inconsistent medication coverage suggests that carbohydrate-reduced nutritional therapy with longitudinal clinical support may remain clinically relevant across the variable medication trajectories encountered in routine obesity care.
Given the observational design, however, the independent contribution of VINT cannot be established.

Taken together, these findings support conceptualizing IOM-based obesity treatment as a longitudinal and evolving care trajectory rather than a conventional prescription-centered approach characterized by intermittent clinical touchpoints and limited support between visits for navigating nutrition, adherence, persistence, tolerability, dose changes, switching, and treatment interruptions.

In this study, both pathways included telemedicine infrastructure, clinician oversight, behavioral support, and access to IOM pharmacotherapy, while individualized carbohydrate-reduced nutrition therapy was the key additional component of VINT+IOM.

The consistently greater weight loss observed with VINT+IOM, including among participants with prior GLP-1 exposure and across heterogeneous medication-use patterns, supports the potential incremental value of integrating individualized nutrition therapy within medication-supported obesity care.

Importantly, 12-month program retention was high in both pathways (77% with VINT+IOM and 72% with IOM only), suggesting that structured carbohydrate-reduced nutritional therapy can be integrated with GLP-1-based pharmacotherapy while maintaining sustained participant engagement.
These findings are consistent with previous real-world evidence demonstrating sustained engagement with VINT delivered independently of GLP-1-based pharmacotherapy (36).

text.text: These findings should be interpreted in the context of the observational study design.

Treatment pathway selection was not randomized, and residual confounding, including differences in motivation, engagement, or other unmeasured characteristics, may have contributed to the observed between-group differences; therefore, the independent effect of VINT cannot be established.

Although both pathways included health coach support, coaching Nutrients 2025, 17, x FOR PEER REVIEW22 of 36 frequency and intensity were not formally compared, and differences in coaching contact, particularly the dietary support provided in VINT+IOM, may have contributed to the observed differences.

Medication selection, adherence, dose escalation, switching, and treatment duration were determined during routine clinical care rather than standardized by protocol, and analyses requiring continued pathway engagement and available weight measurements may have introduced selection bias toward more engaged participants.

Because dose and duration of exposure were not randomized, the contribution of medication exposure cannot be separated from that of the nutrition pathway, and we did not evaluate dose-response relationships.
Sex analyses were exploratory: they used absolute weight rather than percent change, included only 36-53 men per tirzepatide subgroup.

We could not estimate effects for one participant with a third gender category, and we lacked data on menopausal or hormonal status, body composition, energy expenditure and dietary adherence, so we could not test the mechanisms that may underlie sex differences.
Comparison with randomized trials and external real-world cohorts should therefore be considered contextual rather than direct.
Finally, 12 months may be insufficient to characterize maximal weight loss or longer-term trajectories, particularly among participants initiating and titrating IOMs after enrollment.

Longer follow-up is needed to determine weight-loss plateau and durability, medication continuation or discontinuation, and whether the differences observed between nutritional treatment pathways persist over time.

Within this model, participants receiving IOMs may engage in either Virta Individualized Nutrition Therapy (VINT), which emphasizes personalized carbohydrate reduction with continuous monitoring, or IOM only intervention delivered within the same multidisciplinary care infrastructure.

Because the VINT+IOM and IOM-only pathways share digital delivery, clinical oversight, coaching, and medication access while differing primarily in the intensity and individualization of nutritional therapy, they provide an uncommon opportunity to examine the added value of nutritional therapy under routine clinical conditions, with the care infrastructure held largely constant.

The primary objective was to compare 12-month weight loss between VINT+IOM and IOM-only among GLP-1-naïve participants receiving a single GLP-1-based active pharmaceutical ingredient (semaglutide or tirzepatide) during follow-up and remaining engaged in a single prescription pathway for at least 9 months.

This analysis was intended to evaluate the additional weight loss associated with integrating carbohydrate-reduced nutritional therapy with GLP-1-based pharmacotherapy compared with pharmacotherapy alone.

Ancillary analyses examined weight-loss outcomes in the overall prescription cohort and across additional medication exposure subgroups, including the broader GLP-1-naïve population, participants with prior GLP-1 exposure, and those who switched medication ingredients during follow-up.

Among participants with prior GLP-1 exposure, cumulative weight loss from the pre-GLP-1 reference weight was also evaluated to contextualize additional reductions achieved during program participation.
Longitudinal weight trajectories were examined to characterize the pattern of weight reduction over 12 months, including changes between 6 and 12 months.

Secondary objectives included characterizing medication utilization patterns, dose distribution and escalation, medication switching, adherence, and reported side effects, as well as exploring associations between medication use patterns and weight-loss outcomes, and changes in HbA1c as an exploratory outcome.
This study advances existing knowledge in three ways.

First, it compares individualized carbohydrate-reduced nutritional therapy plus IOM with IOM alone within a single care infrastructure, isolating nutrition support as the main difference between pathways, although residual confounding cannot be excluded.
Second, it characterizes real-world medication patterns, including ingredient switching and prior GLP-1 exposure, and relates them to weight outcomes.
These factors are typically excluded or minimized in controlled trials and are rarely captured in claims-based realworld studies, yet they are essential for understanding obesity care in practice.

Third, it describes real-world program retention, medication coverage, and treatment patterns (dosing, escalation, and switching), and shows how a continuous remote care model can accommodate these trajectories while supporting weight loss through 12 months.

Continuous variables are presented as means ± standard deviations (SD) or medians with interquartile ranges (IQR), as appropriate, whereas categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages.

Baseline characteristics were compared between treatment pathways using Student's t test or the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for continuous variables and the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables, as appropriate.

Longitudinal linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate adjusted body weight trajectories and estimated marginal means (EMMs) with 95% confidence intervals at program enrollment, 6 months, and 12 months.

Models included time, treatment pathway, and their interaction, with adjustment for baseline age, sex, BMI, GLP-1 medication use, and HbA1c to account for differences in enrollment characteristics between treatment pathways.
Participant-level random intercepts were included to account for repeated measurements within individuals.

Adjusted weight change from program enrollment to 12 months was estimated for each treatment pathway and prespecified subgroup, allowing comparisons of weight-loss outcomes while accounting for measured baseline differences between groups.

To examine sex differences, we extended the adjusted linear mixed effect models (random participant intercept; adjusted for age, baseline HbA1c and baseline BMI) with time × sex, time × sex × pathway, time × sex × medication, and time Nutrients 2025, 17, x FOR PEER REVIEW11 of 36 × sex × pathway × medication terms.

Sex-specific adjusted means and changes from program start were estimated with model-based marginal means, and differences in change between women and men were tested within each medication-pathway group.
Analyses included women and men only.
HbA1c was analyzed as an exploratory outcome in the primary single-ingredient, GLP-1-naïve cohort, restricted to participants with at least one available HbA1c value.

HbA1c was modeled with a linear mixed-effects model including time (enrollment, 6 months, 12 months), treatment pathway, medication (semaglutide or tirzepatide), and their threeway interaction, with adjustment for baseline age, sex, and BMI.
Baseline HbA1c was not included as a covariate because it was the first observation of the outcome.
Participant-level random intercepts accounted for repeated measurements.

Observed absolute weight change, percentage weight loss, and average monthly weight loss (calculated descriptively as adjusted 12-month weight change divided by 12 months) were summarized using available body weight measurements within each follow-up window.
Between-group comparisons of observed weight outcomes were performed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
Weight-loss responder analyses evaluated the proportions of participants achieving ≥5%, ≥10%, ≥15%, and ≥20% weight loss at 12 months.
Differences in responder proportions between pathways were compared using the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate.
